The SMART methodology provides a structured and systemic framework for categorizing and modeling requirements. However, its practical application remains limited in the absence of dedicated software support capable of operationalizing its hybrid taxonomy and endogenous requirement structure. Existing requirement management tools offer storage and traceability features but do not integrate SMART-specific categorization principles.
This proposal presents the development of

a support system designed to implement the SMART approach in a structured and guided manner. By translating theoretical concepts into functional software components, the system aims to enhance consistency, traceability, and usability in endogenous requirement engineering tasks.

Although the implementation will focus on a prototype-level system within the defined scope, it establishes a foundation for future extensions and potential integration of more advanced analytical features. The project therefore contributes to bridging the gap between the conceptual rigor of SMART and its structured digital application.

This chapter presents a review of existing approaches and tools related to requirement categorization and management. The aim is to analyze how requirements are currently handled in practice and to identify the limitations of these approaches in supporting structured categorization.

Requirements engineering is widely recognized as a fundamental area in software engineering. The quality of requirements directly affects system reliability, maintainability, and overall project success. According to the Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge (SWEBOK), requirement specification, validation, and management are essential activities throughout the software development lifecycle.
Traditional approaches classify requirements into functional and non-functional types which is useful but does not provide enough structure to represent relationships between system components

The SMART methodology (Systemic Approach to Categorizing and Modeling Requirements) provides an organized way to classify and manage requirements. It builds on the Requirements Reference Framework (R2F), which offers a broad view of software systems by including not only the system itself but also its development and operational environments.

In R2F, requirements are linked to clearly defined subjects that represent different parts of the system. These subjects cover software elements such as functions, data, user interfaces, and technical interfaces, as well as aspects of the development environment like processes, tools, human support, and cognitive factors. It also considers the operational environment, including users, procedures, and conditions under which the system is used. This wide perspective helps in analyzing requirements not just based on functionality, but also in relation to the context in which the system is built and used.

SMART introduces a mixed (hybrid) classification approach that goes beyond simply dividing requirements into functional and non-functional types. Instead, it allows requirements to be categorized across multiple dimensions and levels of detail. Requirements can be broken down step by step, from general concepts to more specific elements, making them clearer and more structured. This process ensures that each requirement is linked to a specific subject within the R2F framework.

One of the main strengths of SMART is its structured and rule-based classification method. Requirements are categorized based on predefined rules and relationships rather than random labeling. This helps reduce confusion and improves consistency. The hierarchical structure also makes it easier to navigate requirements and understand how different parts of the system are connected.

In addition, SMART takes into account quality aspects such as usability, reliability, and safety, along with constraints like technical, economic, and cultural factors. This makes it possible to model requirements in a way that reflects both system behavior and real-world conditions.

However, despite its solid theoretical background, SMART is still mostly conceptual. Its practical use is limited because there are no specialized tools that fully support its classification approach. As a result, analysts often have to apply it manually using general tools, which can lead to inconsistencies and make the process less efficient. To address these limitations, the proposed SMART-S2D system aims to provide a practical implementation of the SMART methodology within a structured and guided software environment.
Traditional requirement classification usually separates requirements into two main types:
. Functional requirements define what a system should do

such as handling inputs, producing outputs, or carrying out specific tasks and services. On the other hand, non-functional requirements describe how the system performs these tasks, including qualities like performance, usability, reliability, security, and scalability. This way of classifying requirements is widely used because it is straightforward, easy to understand, and practical in both academic settings and real-world applications.

However, despite how common this approach is, it has clear limitations in terms of depth and structure. It does not clearly show the relationships between different parts of the system, nor does it explain how external factors
like technical constraints or operating environments
affect the requirements. In many situations, requirements are written at a high level without being broken down into smaller, more precise components.

Because of this, the method often depends heavily on the analyst’s judgment when identifying and organizing requirements. This reliance can create inconsistencies, ambiguity, and differences in how various stakeholders interpret the same requirements. In addition, the absence of a clear hierarchy or formal structure makes it harder to trace requirements, ensure consistency, and manage them efficiently
scale systems. These challenges point to the need for more organized and systematic methods of requirement classification.

: The ability to decompose requirements into precise atomic elements that represent specific system subjects, enabling detailed and unambiguous classification.
The ability to incorporate development and operational environments (e.g., hardware, software platforms, external systems) into requirement categorization.
: The ability to track relationships between requirements and their corresponding system elements, ensuring consistency and facilitating impact analysis.
: The degree to which the categorization process produces uniform and repeatable results, either through user discipline or system-guided rules.
: The level of rigor and formal definition in the categorization process, including the use of models, frameworks, and standardized structures.
The ability to browse, explore, and retrieve requirements efficiently through structured navigation mechanisms and search functionalities.

Although Jira is a standard choice for tracking project tasks, it reveals major architectural shortcomings when evaluated for formal systems engineering. We can break down the fundamental differences between Jira’s workflow and the proposed SMART-S2D framework into three primary areas:

In terms of Functional Distinction, Jira provides a basic manual labeling system for issues, but it lacks any internal logic to properly validate or separate Functional Requirements (the "what") from Non-Functional Requirements (the "how"). While a user can choose between a "Story" and a "Task," the tool itself does not recognize the technical dependencies between these categories.
Jira Issue Type Selection providing basic Functional Distinction

Furthermore, Jira’s organizational effectiveness is limited by a project-management hierarchy that prioritizes delivery schedules over technical architecture. Unlike the SMART-S2D system's Hybrid Taxonomy—which organizes requirements through semantic roles like Subject, Action, and Condition—Jira’s classification is purely for administrative tracking. Its Hierarchical Navigation Tree is also Limited; it relies on a shallow "Epic-to-Story" structure as shown in the Timeline view, which cannot handle the deep decomposition needed for complex engineering systems.
: Shallow Hierarchical Structure in Jira Timeline View
Ultimately, Jira is built for monitoring progress, whereas SMART-S2D is designed to support a full architectural breakdown from broad system goals down to specific atomic components.

A major technical shortcoming in Jira is the lack of automated governance during the initial requirement entry phase. Since Jira relies on standard, open-ended text fields, it is rated Wrong for both Atomic Refinement and Guided Categorization. The tool offers no built-in linguistic checks or "SMART Wizard" to stop users from entering vague or compound requirements.

As the interface shows, the platform depends entirely on the user’s own input without checking if the requirement follows SMART standards or R2F structural rules. IBM DOORS is a high-level industrial platform specialized in maintaining complex traceability across large-scale projects. While it provides more depth than basic project management software like Jira, it remains a general-purpose environment that lacks the specialized systemic intelligence inherent in the SMART-S2D system. The following analysis contrasts IBM DOORS with the SMART-S2D framework through three integrated perspectives:

In IBM DOORS, the classification of requirements relies heavily on manual entry through custom attributes or partitioned modules. Since the tool lacks an embedded reference framework like R2F, it cannot autonomously differentiate between a core software function and an environmental constraint. This forces users to define these parameters manually, which frequently results in inconsistent or subjective taxonomies.

By contrast, SMART-S2D is built upon a native hybrid taxonomy. It applies a rigorous structural logic that automatically organizes requirements based on their specific relationship to the software and its surrounding environment, ensuring a clear and standardized distinction between functional and non-functional requirements from the start.

IBM DOORS essentially functions as an open "blank canvas." It offers no built-in linguistic validation or "SMART Wizard" to intercept the entry of ambiguous, multi-part, or poorly formatted requirements. Consequently, the precision of decomposition—ensuring a requirement reaches its "atomic" level—is dependent entirely on the individual analyst's skill level and manual oversight.

SMART-S2D, however, employs a guided elicitation workflow. It functions as a methodological supervisor, funneling each requirement through a mandatory refinement process. This system ensures that every entry is broken down into its most basic atomic subject and verified against SMART criteria before it is accepted into the database.

Navigation within DOORS follows a traditional folder-and-file structure (Database Explorer), and its retrieval features are primarily administrative, focusing on project tracking and ownership. While it supports XML exporting, the resulting files are "flat," containing raw text without the semantic metadata required for technical modeling.

SMART-S2D improves on this by offering a navigation tree strictly aligned with the SMART subject hierarchy (distinguishing between Software and the Operation Environment). It facilitates "Model-Ready" retrieval, allowing users to filter requirements by technical roles such as "Action" or "Condition." Furthermore, its XML output is specifically engineered for R2F interoperability, enabling the automated generation of system architecture diagrams—a capability not supported by DOORS.

To evaluate existing tools and approaches, several key features related to requirement categorization and management are considered. These features reflect the ability of each tool to support structured and systematic handling of requirements:
: Ability to distinguish between different types of requirements.
: Support for multi-level categorization beyond simple classification.
: Ability to refine requirements into detailed atomic elements.
: Support for enforcing structured categorization rules.
: Ability to browse and explore requirements through structured relationships.
: Support for searching and filtering requirements using multiple attributes.
: Ability to generate structured and shareable requirement documentation.

The comparison highlights the differences between traditional requirement classification, informal tools, structured management systems, and theoretical frameworks for requirement categorization. The traditional functional and non-functional classification provides a simple and widely used way to separate what the system should do from the quality constraints it should satisfy. However, this classification is often too broad and does not provide enough detail to support deeper requirement organization, refinement, or navigation.

Spreadsheets provide a flexible way to document requirements but lack structured categorization, hierarchical organization, and consistency. Tools such as Jira and IBM DOORS improve requirement management through traceability and workflow control, but they rely mainly on user-defined labels and do not enforce a formal categorization model.

In contrast, the SMART framework introduces a more structured and systematic approach based on a hybrid taxonomy and the R2F model. Compared with the traditional functional/non-functional classification, SMART provides more detailed requirement subjects and supports hierarchical
categorization, making it easier to classify, refine, and manage requirements consistently. However, its practical use is limited due to the lack of dedicated software support.
This gap between theoretical capability and practical implementation motivates the development of a support system such as SMART-S2D.

Requirement categorization using the SMART methodology is well-supported in theory. The methodology defines clear hierarchical structures and relies on the R2F framework to guide how requirements are classified from within the system itself. These features make it a strong candidate for managing complex requirement sets in a structured and repeatable way.

However, when it comes to actual tool support, the situation is different. No existing requirement management system has been built to reflect how SMART organizes requirements. The hierarchical structures specific to the methodology are not implemented in any current tool, and the logic behind R2F-based endogenous categorization is not enforced anywhere in practice. Because of this, analysts who work with SMART must apply its concepts through manual interpretation, making judgment calls that are not guided or verified by any system.

This creates real problems. When categorization depends on individual interpretation, different analysts will inevitably apply the methodology differently, especially in cases that are not straightforward. Over time, and across larger projects, these differences add up. The consistency that the methodology is supposed to provide starts to break down, and the process becomes harder to manage and scale.

This gap between the theoretical strength of SMART and the lack of tool support for it is the core motivation behind SMART-S2D. The system is not meant to change the methodology itself but to implement it in a way that removes the reliance on manual effort and makes consistent application possible across different users and project contexts.

In conclusion, this chapter reviewed the main concepts, methods, and tools related to requirement categorization and management. The literature shows that while traditional classifications such as functional and non-functional requirements are widely used, they are often too broad to support detailed categorization and refinement. Existing tools such as spreadsheets, Jira, and IBM DOORS provide useful support for documentation, tracking, and traceability, but they do not enforce a formal requirement categorization methodology.

The SMART methodology, supported by the R2F framework, provides a more structured approach through hierarchical and taxonomy-based categorization. However, the lack of dedicated tool support limits its practical application. Therefore, this research identifies a clear gap between the theoretical strength of SMART and its implementation in real software tools. This gap motivates the development of SMART-S2D as a support system for structured requirement writing, categorization, retrieval, and management

In this chapter, we implement the SMART methodology to create a systematic foundation for our SMART-S2D tool. At the heart of this method is the R2F (Referential Requirement Framework), enabling us to break down the software system into its essential elements and categorize requirements according to their source and impact. The Software Subject serves as the foundational element of the R2F framework, defining the internal parameters and limits of the product by separating system-specific needs from those shaped by external operational or developmental environments.

The class diagram illustrates the structure of the SMART-S2D Requirement Management System and the relationships between its main classes. The Requirement class represents the core component and is categorized into Endogenous Requirement and Exogenous Requirement. Endogenous requirements are further specialized into development, software, and operation requirements, while software requirements are divided into function, data, user interface, and technical interface requirements. The diagram also models the SMART taxonomy using generic and specific subjects and factors. In addition, supporting classes such as project, software, system, and company are included to represent the organizational environment of the system
Requirement Categorization Sequence Diagram shows how a requirement entered by an analyst is processed and categorized step by step:
The Analyst opens the categorization page in the Web UI and enters requirement details.
The Web UI sends these details to the Categorization Controller.
The controller asks the SMART Engine to suggest atomic (basic) categories using subjects and taxonomy from the Database.

provides a conceptual overview of the system’s data architecture, focusing on the logical flow from high-level categorization to technical execution. The model is centered around the Software entity, which acts as the primary technical foundation. Generic Subjects are decomposed into Specific Subjects, which in turn serve as the parent categories for individual Requirements; these requirements then link directly to the Software they define. Internally, the software contains various Systems, while externally, it is implemented by one or more Projects. Finally, the Company entity provides organizational oversight by managing these projects. This structure ensures that every requirement is traceable through its specific subject matter to the exact software components and corporate projects responsible for its delivery.

These requirements, along with technical Systems, are consolidated under the Software entity, serving as the central technical foundation. Finally, the Project entity integrates the organizational layer by linking a specific piece of software to its managing Company, ensuring that every requirement is traceable from its conceptual origin to its final software delivery and project ownership.

These requirements are tied directly to the Software entity, which also serves as a parent to various Systems. Finally, the Project entity integrates the technical and organizational layers by connecting the software to its managing Company, ensuring full traceability from broad subject matter down to specific technical implementations and corporate ownership

The UI Prototype section presents the visual design and interaction flow of the SMART-S2D system. The purpose of this prototype is to demonstrate how users can manage software requirements using the SMART methodology and the R2F-based requirement categorization approach. The prototype was designed as a high-fidelity web application to show the main screens, navigation structure, requirement-writing workflow, taxonomy selection process, and requirement repository features.

The SMART-S2D prototype focuses on the software requirements branch of endogenous requirements. Since the current project scope is limited to software requirements, the active taxonomy includes four main categories: Function requirements, Data requirements, User Interface requirements, and Technical Interface requirements. Operation requirements and Development requirements are displayed as future taxonomy branches but are disabled in the current prototype. This helps communicate that the system is designed to be expandable while keeping the implemented prototype focused and realistic.

The prototype begins with a workspace page where users can create, join, or open a company and manage related projects. This structure reflects how requirements are usually organized in real software engineering environments, where work belongs to a company or team and each project contains its own requirement repository. Users can create projects, open existing projects, update project information, and manage requirements within the selected project.

After opening a project, users can access the project dashboard, which summarizes requirement information such as total requirements, draft requirements, requirements needing review, approved requirements, and rejected requirements. This dashboard gives project managers, analysts, and other users a quick overview of the requirement status and supports requirement monitoring during the development process.

One of the main interfaces in the prototype is the SMART Requirement Template page. This page guides users through writing requirements using a structured template rather than relying only on free text. The template follows the SMART/R2F writing style by separating the Generic Subject, Specific Subject, Specific Subject statement, and Specific Subject model. This helps users produce clearer and more consistent software requirement statements. The system also provides rule-based validation and category suggestions to support requirement classification without using AI.

The prototype also includes a taxonomy page that visually presents the software requirement taxonomy and allows users to understand how requirements are categorized under the SMART structure. In addition, the requirements repository and search pages allow users to view saved requirements, filter them, open requirement details, and edit requirement information such as title, category, priority, status, and requirement statement. This supports requirement retrieval and refinement, which are important parts of structured requirement management.

The reports page allows users to export project requirements in supported formats such as XML and DOCX. These exports are intended to support academic demonstrations, requirement reviews, and documentation sharing. The Admin/Settings area provides administrative access for managing system-related functions in future development phases.

Overall, the SMART-S2D UI prototype demonstrates a specialized requirement management system rather than a general task management tool. Its interface is designed around SMART-based requirement writing, software requirement taxonomy navigation, structured categorization, project-based organization, and requirement retrieval. By presenting the complete set of prototype screens, the design illustrates how SMART-S2D can help users create, classify, manage, and review software requirements in a more systematic and academically grounded way.
